text:
Recent evaluation research supports separating user experience from offline ranking accuracy. The [2024 Dagstuhl evaluation report](https://dbis.uibk.ac.at/sites/default/files/2024-11/DagRep.14.5.58.pdf) emphasizes incomplete, biased feedback, per-user outcome distributions, and uncertainty around averages. A practical proposed taxonomy—not an established validated scale—is: **choose-now appeal**, **mere relatedness without expressed intent**, **explicit mismatch**, and **insufficient evidence**. Preserve supporting feedback excerpts; do not convert missing evidence into dislike or infer unobserved diversity/conformity traits. Twenty users, five per category, provide exploratory cases; simulator judgments remain simulated evidence about those users.

Connect explicit preference pairs to the trained model’s score margin, Δ = s(preferred) − s(rejected), with candidates and history fixed. Negative margins identify disagreement; relatedness alone cannot establish a preference pair. The [original HSTU paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) motivates inspecting relative attention bias, attention aggregation, and feature interaction. Within the single fitted model, temporarily disable implemented components individually and measure paired margin/rank changes. These are sensitivity probes; inference-time interventions can create distribution shift and cannot establish that retraining without a component would improve performance. Proposed controls: identity interventions, shuffled feedback-to-user assignments, and matched random history perturbations; never deploy perturbed copies as an ensemble.

Report user-level paired outcomes, category counts, and leave-one-user-out sensitivity; bootstrap users rather than treating recommendations from one user as independent observations. With five users per category, uncertainty estimates remain fragile. Use feedback and component sensitivity to generate hypotheses, retaining the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10 as the sole selection criterion. Full-catalog qualitative recommendations and sampled-candidate validation measure different settings; neither substitutes for the other.
